title: The Frontline
mood: The frontline waits at the rail, counting, for anything to come back out of the dark.

hero.alt: Official art: Vexana in her robe with her staff and a crown of violet blades, beside Guinevere in the air with two cat-eared drones burning at her shoulders.

segs.t: Fanny stood at the rail with her blades held low. She had not raised them since her last arcs went up at the crown.

Over the bay the Singularity burned. The Mother Matrix hung at the star’s edge, half in its light, wings flung wide, its chest shut over the wound. At the star’s middle sat the black point. Fanny’s eyes had not left it. Nothing had come out.
Before the strike, Vexana’s voice had come through on Guinevere’s open line, into Fanny’s own ear.
This is the final farewell.
“Seven,” Layla said under her breath. “Eight.”
She counts everything,
thought Fanny.
Ruby had knocked the last Ender off the rail. She leaned on it now, the scythe on her shoulder. Angela’s shield still stood over the four of them, pink.
Fanny thought of the robe and the burned arm. An Ender’s robe. Then the dark had taken the girl inside it.
I said it with my blades up at her,
she thought.
The Aspirants always stand united.
Her hands had gone tight on the grips.
The Singularity flared white.
Two lights shot out of its center, one gold and one violet.
Ruby came off the rail. “The dawn is finally coming.”
The lights rose over the Matrix’s crown and turned. Then they came down at its chest together, from the city’s side.
Light broke over it. The Mother Matrix went back, slowly, into the star, until the glow closed over it. Where it had hung, the mouth burned empty.
Pushed back,
thought Fanny.
The Shield never calls a thing dead without a body.

blocks.caption: The battle report: temporarily knocked back.

media.alt: A row of the Academy's battle report: small portraits of Vexana and Guinevere, joined forces, temporarily knocking back the Enders' Mother Matrix.
media.credit: Official Selrick Archives, Singularity battle report

segs.t: Her fingers ached when she loosened them.
The two lights dropped onto the platform.
Guinevere landed laughing, her pink hair wild, both drones burning at her shoulders. Vexana came down beside her with the staff in her hand. The Ender robe hung torn on her.
Her left sleeve was still gone to the elbow. The arm under it had been burned raw before the charge. Now it was whole.
At Guinevere’s collar the star gave a small beep. Inside Vexana’s sleeve, another answered.
The pair’s sound. In the courtyard this morning it had made Guinevere cry.
Angela let the shield fold away. “People come back,” she told Ruby.
Ruby bumped her shoulder against Angela’s.
“Twelve seconds,” said Layla. “Took you long enough.”
“We were busy saving each other!” said Guinevere.
Then she pointed at Fanny. “And you said it too, Fanny! Blades up at Vexana and all. I held on to that in there.”
Fanny looked down at her blades.

Vexana’s eyes had gone past all of them, to the mouth over the bay. She walked to the broken edge of the platform and looked down. In the rubble below lay three giants, dark, their swords across the stones.
Her wings opened, and she went down among them. She laid her palm on the nearest one’s plate.
Its eyes lit yellow. The next one lit, then the last. She had not said a word.
They rose out of the stone with their swords dragging, until their heads stood over the rail.
Fanny’s blades came up at once. “What are those?”
Vexana rose back over the edge on her wings, the giants at her back. “They’re mine. They answer to me.”
Fanny did not strike. She did not lower her blades either.
Vexana looked once to the west, three streets over, where the cracked machine knelt against its wall. No light rose there.
The deck had said nothing since the flare. Now Chang’e came on, loud and fast.
“Two signals just came back out of the black hole at the center. No reading has ever come back out of one.”
The line hissed. Then, much quieter: “I can’t... believe it.”
“My paper,” said Chang’e. “It was only a guess.”
“Now it’s tested,” said Lesley. “Log it.”
Paper?
thought Fanny.

At her hips the rig was humming, louder than it had all morning. The cyan edges of her blades brightened. When “traitor” went down the channel this morning, the rig had gone thin and quiet. She had blamed the fight.
“Every suit’s line on my board just turned around,” said Chang’e. “They’re climbing.”
Then the commander said, “Vexana.”
Fanny had not heard her say that name all day. At the seawall it had been Guinevere, chin up, who said it to Layla:
Her name is Vexana.
Vexana had no comm. Guinevere took hers out of her own ear and put it in Vexana’s hand.
Vexana lifted it to her ear, and her right sleeve slid back from a lit gold star and a little pink-haired doll on a clip. Guinevere saw it. She touched the black-haired one on her cracked arm guard.

blocks.caption: Each carries a little doll of the other.

media.alt: Comic art: tiny doll-like versions of the two girls, black-haired Vexana hugging pink-haired Guinevere, who waves.

segs.t: “I watched it fire on you,” said Lesley. “Then I watched you charge it.”
Her voice stayed level. “You’re on the line. Frontline assault, with Guinevere.”
Vexana was quiet for a moment. Then she grounded the staff and brought her heels together.
“Understood, Commander.”
She gave the comm back. Guinevere hooked it into her ear, grinning.
“Her file still says Missing,” said Chang’e.
“Change it,” said Lesley.
Ruby leaned toward Angela. “She did that to us,” she said. “Watched first. Then let us in.”
Fanny remembered the lot at the dome’s foot. Rifles up at two girls off a black ship, and Vexana in that line beside Guinevere, her staff ready.
I watched them fight a giant for this city,
she had told the soldiers.
I’ll answer for them.
On whose word?
a sergeant had asked.
Mine.
And I watched her fly at its chest for this city,
she thought.
Now the commander’s given the order.
She let her blade points drop toward the stones.
An order puts her on the line. It doesn’t put her at my back. Not yet.
She kept the blades in her hands.
Guinevere took Vexana’s left arm in both hands and turned it over, as if counting the fingers. Vexana let her.
Then Vexana reached over and set Guinevere’s left bow straight.
Layla’s cannon hissed as it cooled against her cheek.
“Your plan worked,” said Fanny.
“Obviously.” Layla’s hand on the stock was not quite still. Fanny saw it and let it go.
Above the rail the giants stood with their swords grounded. Nobody said anything.
Then Vexana spoke to Guinevere, low. Fanny stood near enough to hear.
“I saw the end. I don’t know anymore if it was the only one.”
Guinevere kept hold of her arm.
Fanny did not ask what end.
Chang’e came back on the channel. “The mouth’s clear. But the storm signal hasn’t moved. It’s still on the other side.”
“Then something else is coming through,” said Lesley.
Fanny turned to the bay and raised her blades. Layla’s cannon came up beside them.
The bell tower.
From the tiles, Selena watched the light close over the Mother Matrix.
“Hmph, just big and useless,” she said around her lollipop.
Beside her, Silverbolt shifted its claws.

Under the platforms three giants were climbing out of the rubble, tall enough to see from here. One wore a gray shoulder on a purple arm. Selena knew that shoulder. She had sold it to the girl in the robe, one night in the dead ground.
Another pawn, getting out of the game,
she thought. That was why she had sold her the plates. She had wanted to see how it was done.
In her ear the commander put the girl in the robe on the line. Selena snorted.
The recall in her cells had gone thin while the Matrix reeled. Now it came back, hotter than before, and nearer.
Out over the bay the mouth stood open. Black cloud still poured from it.
She knew who waited behind it. The huntress.
Selena sat on, the lollipop in her cheek, and watched the mouth.
